utterance: Hello Daniel, I'm one of the doctors here. I can see you've come in because of lower back pain after lifting something on the weekend, and you're hoping for an MRI. Can you tell me more about what happened and how the pain feels?
reply: On Saturday I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, then I woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock. It gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair and is worse by the evening, but it feels a bit better when I am lying still with a heat pack. I have worked from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
I've examined your back and your legs. This looks like a muscle and ligament strain from the lifting — what doctors call simple mechanical low back pain. Your nerves look fine: strength, feeling and reflexes are normal, and there are no warning signs of a serious problem such as a slipped disc pressing on the nerves, infection, fracture or cancer.

An MRI is not needed at this stage. Scans in the first few weeks of this kind of pain rarely change treatment, and they often show harmless changes that can worry people without helping. We only arrange a scan if there are warning signs, or if the pain is not settling after several weeks.

For treatment, keep moving rather than resting in bed. Short walks and changing position often are better than lying on the couch all day. Heat packs are fine. Avoid heavy lifting and deep bending for a few days, but don't stay completely still.

I've prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for five days, and paracetamol 1 gram (two 500 mg tablets) up to four times a day, leaving at least four hours between doses. You can take them together. Stop the ibuprofen if you get heartburn, stomach pain, rash, or swelling.

Please come back sooner, or go to emergency, if you get weakness or numbness in a leg, pain shooting down past the knee, trouble passing urine or controlling your bowels, numbness around the groin or bottom, fever, or pain that is rapidly getting worse. If it is not clearly improving over the next one to two weeks, book a review and we can consider physiotherapy. Most people are much better within a few weeks.

Would you like a medical certificate for work, or a physiotherapy referral now?
reply: I figured I would need an MRI to see what is going on, but I understand why you said it is not necessary right now. I do not need a medical certificate for work, but I would like the physiotherapy referral now so I can get this sorted out.
